--- title: "Partial effects" description: "A partial dependence plot draws how a model's prediction changes along one input, averaged over every station, and ICE curves draw the same change station by station. On the survey they show where a random forest predicts the most animals, and that the temperature hump appears at nearly every station." order: 2 categories: [interpretation] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## Partial effects draw how a prediction changes along one input [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) says how much a model relies on an input, but not whether the prediction rises or falls with it, or where it peaks. **Partial effects** draw that shape: how the model's prediction changes as one input moves. This page draws them two ways, averaged over every station and station by station, and shows what each can and cannot tell you. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A partial dependence plot averages the curve over every station A **partial dependence plot** starts from the data the model was fitted to. Set one input to the same value in every row, keep every other input as it was recorded, and predict each row. The average of those predictions is one point on the curve. Repeat for each value along the input's range, and the points make the curve. It works for any model, because it only needs predictions. ::: {.diagram} ![Partial dependence in three steps: give every row the same value of one input and keep the others, predict each row and move the value along its range so each row traces a curve, then average the rows' curves.](img/partial-dependence.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Set one input, every row gets one value: a small table with inputs A, B and C, where every cell of column A reads 40 and the shaded cells of B and C are kept. Predict each row, one ICE curve per row: five orange humped curves of different heights against input A, with a dashed line at 40 marking where each row's prediction was made. Average, the partial dependence: the same five curves in grey with a thick green curve through their middle, their average. A note says that where the rows' curves differ in shape, the average hides it, so look at both."} ::: Setting an input to its extreme values in every row builds stations the survey never had, such as the shallowest depth paired with the coldest water, so the curves on this page run only over the middle 90% of each input's values, where most stations lie. ## ICE curves show the same sweep station by station Before averaging, each row has its own curve: its prediction as the one input moves and the rest of the row stays put. These are **individual conditional expectation (ICE) curves**, and the partial dependence is their average. If they share one shape and differ only in height, the average describes them well. If they peak in different places or cross, the effect of the input depends on the others, an [interaction](../06-assumptions-limitations/linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd), and the average alone would hide it. ## Worked example A random forest of 500 trees, as in [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd), predicts abundance from the six inputs of [Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd) and is fitted to the training sites of the same split by site. Its partial dependence is drawn for the two inputs it relied on most, temperature and depth, then its ICE curves for temperature. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season") split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) forest_recipe <- recipe(reformulate(inputs, "abundance"), data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) forest_model <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |> set_mode("regression") forest <- workflow(forest_recipe, forest_model) |> fit(train) ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.inspection import partial_dependence from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] recipe = ColumnTransformer( [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical)]) # max_features and min_samples_leaf match ranger's defaults model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt", min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=123) forest = Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)]).fit( train[numeric + categorical], train["abundance"]) ``` ::: ::: ### The forest predicts most animals in cool water and at shallow depths Each input is set in turn to 40 values across the middle 90% of its range, and every training station is predicted at each. The partial dependence is the average at each value. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # every training station's prediction with one input set to each of 40 # values over the middle 90% of its range sweep <- function(fitted, input) { ends <- quantile(train[[input]], c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE) map(seq(ends[1], ends[2], length.out = 40), \(level) { swept <- train swept[[input]] <- level tibble(station = swept$station_id, value = level, .pred = predict(fitted, swept)$.pred) }) |> list_rbind() } ice <- list(depth_m = sweep(forest, "depth_m"), temperature_c = sweep(forest, "temperature_c")) # the partial dependence is the average over the stations partial <- map(ice, \(d) summarise(d, .pred = mean(.pred), .by = value)) peak_of <- \(d) d$value[which.max(d$.pred)] tibble(Input = c("Depth (m)", "Temperature (°C)"), `Highest prediction at` = map_dbl(partial, peak_of), `Highest` = map_dbl(partial, \(d) max(d$.pred)), `Lowest` = map_dbl(partial, \(d) min(d$.pred))) |> mutate(across(-Input, \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Input | Highest prediction at| Highest| Lowest| |:----------------|---------------------:|-------:|------:| |Depth (m) | 24.5| 5.7| 3.3| |Temperature (°C) | 7.7| 5.8| 3.0|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # every training station's prediction with one input set to each of 40 # values over the middle 90% of its range def sweep(fitted, column, kind="average"): result = partial_dependence( fitted, train[numeric + categorical], [column], kind=kind, percentiles=(0.05, 0.95), grid_resolution=40) return result["grid_values"][0], result[kind][0] rows = [] for column, name in [("depth_m", "Depth (m)"), ("temperature_c", "Temperature (°C)")]: grid, average = sweep(forest, column) rows.append({"Input": name, "Highest prediction at": grid[average.argmax()], "Highest": average.max(), "Lowest": average.min()}) pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Input | Highest prediction at | Highest | Lowest | |:-----------------|------------------------:|----------:|---------:| | Depth (m) | 37.4 | 4.7 | 2.8 | | Temperature (°C) | 7.8 | 4.9 | 2.9 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} one <- \(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1) curve_plot <- function(which, x_label) { ggplot(partial[[which]], aes(value, .pred)) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.2) + expand_limits(y = 0) + labs(x = x_label, y = "Average prediction\n(individuals)") } curve_plot("depth_m", "Depth (m)") + curve_plot("temperature_c", "Temperature (°C)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The random forest's partial dependence on depth and on temperature, over the middle 90% of each input's values: the average prediction over every training station as one input is set to each value.](partial-effects_files/figure-html/fig-partial-1.png){#fig-partial fig-alt='Two panels of predicted count against an input. Left, depth: the curve is highest, about 5.7 individuals, at the shallowest depth drawn, and falls in steps to about 3.3 at the deepest. Right, temperature: the curve is low in the coldest water, rises steeply between 6 and 7 degrees to a peak of about 5.8 at 7.7 degrees, and falls again in the warmest water.' width=1600} ::: ::: The forest predicts the most animals at 7.7 °C, in cool water, and fewer in both colder and warmer water: temperature has a hump. Depth works one way only: the prediction is highest at 24 m, the shallowest value drawn, and falls by 43% towards 154 m. A single coefficient could not draw the hump; the plot reads both shapes straight off the fitted forest. ### ICE curves show the temperature hump at nearly every station The same sweep, before averaging, gives one curve for each of the 598 training stations. @fig-ice draws them for temperature. For each station, the table below measures the rise from the coldest temperature drawn to the partial dependence's peak, and the fall from there to the warmest. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # each station's rise from the coldest value drawn to the partial # dependence's peak, and its fall from there to the warmest top <- peak_of(partial$temperature_c) changes <- ice$temperature_c |> summarise(rise = .pred[value == top] - first(.pred), fall = .pred[value == top] - last(.pred), .by = station) changes |> pivot_longer(c(rise, fall), names_to = "change", values_to = "size") |> summarise(`Above zero` = percent(mean(size > 0)), Lowest = round(min(size), 1), Median = round(median(size), 1), Highest = round(max(size), 1), .by = change) |> mutate(change = str_to_sentence(change)) |> rename(Change = change) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Change |Above zero | Lowest| Median| Highest| |:------|:----------|------:|------:|-------:| |Rise |100% | 0.0| 2.6| 8.9| |Fall |98% | -0.7| 2.3| 8.3|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} grid, curves = sweep(forest, "temperature_c", kind="individual") # each station's rise from the coldest value drawn to the partial # dependence's peak, and its fall from there to the warmest top = curves.mean(axis=0).argmax() changes = pd.DataFrame({"rise": curves[:, top] - curves[:, 0], "fall": curves[:, top] - curves[:, -1]}) (pd.DataFrame({"Above zero": (changes > 0).mean().map("{:.0%}".format), "Lowest": changes.min().round(1), "Median": changes.median().round(1), "Highest": changes.max().round(1)}) .set_axis(["Rise", "Fall"]) .rename_axis("Change")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | Change | Above zero | Lowest | Median | Highest | |:---------|:-------------|---------:|---------:|----------:| | Rise | 100% | 0.6 | 1.9 | 4.2 | | Fall | 100% | 0.3 | 1.8 | 4.4 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(ice$temperature_c, aes(value, .pred)) + geom_line(aes(group = station), colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.3) + geom_line(data = partial$temperature_c, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.4) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted count (individuals)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![ICE curves for temperature: the random forest's prediction for each training station as its temperature is moved and the rest of the station stays as recorded, with their average, the partial dependence, in blue. Almost every curve rises between 6 and 7 °C, stays high to about 10 °C and then falls; the curves differ mostly in height.](partial-effects_files/figure-html/fig-ice-1.png){#fig-ice fig-alt='Several hundred thin grey curves against temperature from about 4 to 13.5 degrees, most between 1 and 10 predicted individuals, a few reaching 17 to 25. Nearly all are level below about 5.5 degrees, rise between 6 and 7 degrees, stay high with small wiggles to about 10.4 degrees, then drop and level off towards the warm end. Higher curves rise and fall by more. A thick blue curve, their average, runs through the lower middle of the bundle with the same shape, from about 3 up to nearly 6 and back to about 3.4.' width=1400} ::: ::: The curve rises from the coldest water to the partial dependence's peak on all but 1 of the 598 stations, and falls again towards the warmest on all but 14 of the 598 stations. The size of the rise differs far more: half the stations rise by less than 2.6 individuals, the largest by 8.9. Stations where the forest predicts many animals anyway gain most from the right temperature, so the curves share a shape and differ in scale. The partial dependence shows where the hump lies; how large it is depends on the station. ## A curve reads as a response only where its input varies on its own A partial dependence plot and its ICE curves are a faithful picture of what a model predicts, not a measurement of the species. As [Feature importance](feature-importance.qmd) showed, inputs that carry the same information share the work, and the forest may give an effect to either of them. A curve reads as the species' response only where the data let that input vary on its own. [Interpretable models and surrogates](interpretable-models.qmd) turns to models whose parts can be read directly. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **partial dependence plot** sets one input to each value in turn in every row, predicts, and averages. It works for any model and shows the direction and shape of an effect. - **ICE curves** are the same sweep for each row before averaging. Curves that share a shape show the average describes them; curves that peak in different places show an interaction. - Draw the curves where the data are: a sweep pairs each value with every row's other inputs, including combinations the survey never had. - On the survey the forest predicted most animals in cool water and in shallow water, and the temperature hump appeared at nearly every station, at different heights. - The curves describe the model; they describe the species only where the data let the input vary on its own. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Draw the partial dependence of `substrate`: set every training station to each level in turn and average the predictions. Which level does the forest predict most animals on? 2. Draw the ICE curves for depth. Do the stations share one shape, as they did for temperature?
